core_obligations: Reduce to a finite surjective chart (proof lines 1672-1682): replacing X by a quasi-compact neighbourhood of x one may assume X quasi-compact, separated and Noetherian; choose a scheme U with a finite surjective morphism onto X and let R be the fibre product, so that one obtains a groupoid scheme with finite source and target and U Noetherian and separated; the finitely many points of U mapping to x have local rings of dimension at most one by the dimension comparison for quasi-finite morphisms.

Produce an invariant affine open (proof lines 1684-1690): the orbit of those finitely many points is contained in an R-invariant affine open W by the groupoid lemma on orbits of dimension at most one.

Conclude that a neighbourhood of x is an affine scheme (proof lines 1690-1698): since the finite surjective morphism is closed, its induced map on spaces is submersive, so the image of W is open and there is an open subspace X' with W -> X' surjective and finite; the image of an invariant affine open under such a morphism is an affine scheme, so X' is an open subspace of X containing x which is a scheme.
proof_roadmap: Make the situation quasi-compact and Noetherian and choose a finite surjective scheme over the space.
Control the dimensions of the local rings of the finitely many points over x and find an invariant affine open containing them.
Use submersiveness of the finite surjective map to descend that affine open to an affine open subspace of the space.
difficulty_reason: The lemma proves that a point of a separated locally Noetherian algebraic space whose local ring has dimension at most one has an open neighbourhood which is a scheme (statement lines 1659-1670). The proof (proof lines 1672-1701) reduces to a quasi-compact Noetherian situation with a finite surjective chart, bounds the dimensions of the local rings of the points over the given point, finds an invariant affine open containing them, and uses submersiveness of the finite surjective map to produce an affine open subspace of the space. H3: a groupoid-theoretic reduction with genuine orbit and dimension control, written out in full.
